Carveyance The Material File

Tree Sap · Soot · Sulfur · Steel

I'm Rubber,
You're Glue

Four postcards of rubber are the only things holding you to the planet. The accidents that made them, the war that almost ran out of them, and the exact speed at which rubber gives up and flies off the rim.

By Jolice Franklyn Fun Facts 56 minute read

I took my kids to the park last weekend and spent most of it doing arithmetic on my own childhood.

The ground was the first thing. When I was small, playgrounds were built over concrete and packed dirt, and every piece of equipment on them was, in retrospect, an object of certain pain. Now the ground is dark, soft and faintly springy, and a child can go down hard and get back up annoyed rather than broken and bleeding.

The see-saw had regulators on it. There is a damper in the middle now, so that when the heavier kid gets bored and hops off, the lighter one does not come down like an anvil. That used to be the entire point of the see-saw, if you were the heavier kid.

The merry-go-round is simply gone. Not modified. Gone.

And then, at the far end, hanging from a chain, entirely unimproved and unregulated by anybody: a tire swing. Not a molded plastic tire swing. An actual tire, off an actual car, with the tread still on it.

There was a line for it. There is always a line for it.

The one piece of playground equipment that survived a half-century of safety engineering is the one made out of a used car part. Nobody designed it. Somebody just had a spare tire and a length of rope, and it turned out to be better than most of the things that were designed.

Which got me thinking about everywhere else the stuff turns up once you start looking. Tires hung over the side of a tugboat, doing the job of a bumper because nothing else absorbs an impact between two steel hulls that cheaply. Surgical gloves. The seals around an aircraft door holding a pressure difference at 38,000 feet. Roofing membranes. Conveyor belts. The bushings under your car, and the vibration mounts under some buildings. The U.S. Tire Manufacturers Association counts natural rubber in more than 40,000 products, and that is before you get to the synthetic half.

Rubber is so thoroughly woven through ordinary life that it even ended up in the playground insult economy. If someone bested you in the term wars of five-year-olds, you always had the nuclear option: I'm rubber, you're glue — whatever you say bounces off me and sticks to you. If that didn't work you redirected the conversation, or you submitted to defeat.

Here is the irony. When it comes to rubber and cars, you want precisely the opposite. You want the rubber to be the glue. You want it to stick.

Do the arithmetic, because it is worse than you think. A contact patch is, to a first approximation, the load divided by the inflation pressure. Take a 4,000 lb car on 35 psi. 4,000 divided by 35 is 114 square inches. Divide by four tires.

28 square inches. Per corner. That is a postcard. Slightly smaller than the palm of your hand.

Four postcards. That is the entire negotiated interface between two tons of engineering and the surface of the planet. Every horsepower figure you have ever been impressed by. Every braking distance in every road test you have ever read. Every corner you have ever taken well and every one you have taken badly. All of it, routed through four rectangles of black polymer roughly the size of a paperback cover.

We spend fortunes on brakes, suspension geometry, torque vectoring and stability control — and then hand the entire conversation over to a ring of tree sap and soot.

Harry Hogge was right

In Days of Thunder, Robert Duvall's crew chief Harry Hogge spends half the film trying to get this through Cole Trickle's head, and eventually gives up on subtlety: "Tires is what wins a race, Cole." He goes on to point out that 40 other drivers manage to finish on the tires they were given.

It plays as a grizzled-veteran line. It is closer to a statement of physics. Everything the engine, the brakes and the driver produce has to be sold to the road through four postcards, and the moment those four postcards give up, nothing else on the car is relevant.

It gets stranger from there. Tire history has a reputation for being tiresome. It is the opposite. It is 180 years of chemists ruining stoves, brothers sabotaging races, one country almost losing a world war over a plantation crop, and a 1,000 mph car that had to throw the rubber away entirely.

Very little of it was planned. Almost none of it was invented when you think it was.

A Hundred Things Pretending to Be One

Bridgestone reckons an average passenger tire contains well over a hundred separate components. Not a hundred grams of rubber. A hundred distinct materials and structures, layered and cured into something that looks, from the outside, like a single object.

It is worth taking one apart.

The tread is the only part that touches the road, and the least important structurally. It is a wear surface — a sacrificial compound tuned for grip, temperature and longevity. The grooving cut into it does one job: evacuate water. A tire does not grip a wet road by squeezing the water out. It grips by giving the water somewhere else to be, at a rate of many liters a second, in the fractions of a moment before the contact patch arrives.

The shoulder strip is the transition between tread and sidewall, and it is where a tire lives or dies in a corner. It carries the load when the car leans, and it runs hotter than anywhere else.

Beneath the tread sits the belt package, and this is where the engineering happens. A layer of steel cord running transverse to the tread. Another layer of steel cord running lengthwise. A cap of nylon fabric over the top. The two steel belts are laid at opposing angles so that they triangulate against one another — pull on one and the other resists. The result is a tread band that is enormously stiff around its circumference and can still flex vertically. That is the whole trick of the radial tire, and we will come back to it.

Below that, the carcass — usually two plies of textile cord, in a radial tire running at ninety degrees to the direction of travel, straight across from bead to bead. The carcass is the skeleton. It contains the air pressure and defines the shape.

Inside everything, the inner liner: a thin layer of halobutyl rubber whose only function in life is to be almost perfectly impermeable to air. It is the reason your tire is still up in the morning. It is also a synthetic, and there is no natural substitute for it. Hold that thought for about 2,000 words.

The sidewall is not structural in the way people assume. In a radial tire it is deliberately supple, because the belts are holding the tread flat and the sidewall's job is to flex, absorb, and stay out of the way. It also carries the markings, and it takes the abuse of every curb you have ever misjudged.

Then the bead, which is the least glamorous and most consequential part of the entire object. The bead wire is a bundle of high-tensile steel hoops. It is what clamps the tire to the rim against a couple of thousand pounds of internal pressure trying to blow it off. The bead filler stiffens the transition from bead to sidewall and tunes the steering response. The bead chafer protects everything from the rim itself, and the rim strip seals the joint.

The tire is not a rubber ring with steel in it. It is a steel and textile pressure vessel, wearing rubber.

None of this existed in 1839. All of it exists because of five ideas — and because of a sixth that nobody ranks, which arrived because a country was about to lose a war.

Before Any of It

A Hoop of Iron and a Prayer

The word tire predates rubber by about 3,000 years, and for most of that time it meant a band that protected the wheel rather than the passenger.

Spoked wooden wheels appear in Western Asia around 2000 BCE, on chariots built by the Sintashta culture. By the Iron Age, wheelwrights were shrinking metal hoops around the outside of those wheels to hold them together and stop them wearing away. That basic design — wood, spokes, an iron band, no cushioning of any kind — lasted until the 19th century.

It also lasted longer into the automotive era than anyone remembers. Open the Sears catalog for 1908, the year Ford launched the Model T, and you will find buggy and wagon wheels at $7.65 per set (about $280 today), over 60,000 sets sold in a season, alongside a Traveler's Big Complete Repair Outfit at $2.95 (about $108). Hickory, in the white, with tires — and the tires in question were steel.

Fun Fact

Solid rubber tires arrived in the 1850s for horse-drawn vehicles, and by the 1870s manufacturers had worked out how to embed wire in the rubber to stop it stretching off the wheel. The first widespread application was on London Hansom cabs, from 1881. Carl Benz used solid rubber on his 1886 Patent Motorwagen, and the rims were outsourced — which technically makes Benz the world's first automobile tire manufacturer, since he built his own.

The Five Breakthroughs

I · Vulcanization

Without it, rubber is not a material. It is a seasonal inconvenience.

Before 1839, rubber was a bad joke that people kept telling anyway. It stretched. It kept water out. It also turned to sticky, foul-smelling gum in summer, and cracked apart in winter. Boots failed. Coats failed. They failed predictably, twice a year, which is somehow worse.

The problem is molecular. Natural rubber is polyisoprene — very long chains, tangled together like cooked spaghetti in a bowl. Tangled, but not tied. Stretch it and the strands slide past one another and stay where you left them. Heat it and they slide too easily: you get goo. Chill it and they stop moving at all: you get something brittle enough to shatter.

Charles Goodyear spent years throwing things at this. Acids, powders, chemicals, heat, whatever was on the shelf. He was not a chemist. He was obsessive, frequently broke, and mostly wrong.

In 1839, working around a hot stove, he got a mixture of rubber and sulfur onto the heat. It should have melted. It hardened. He turned the heat up and it hardened further.

What happened is that the sulfur atoms formed bridges — cross-links — between those long sliding chains. The spaghetti became a net. Vulcanized rubber can still stretch, but it can no longer slide away from itself permanently. The bridges haul it back.

This is what "temperature stable" actually means, and it is worth being precise about, because the phrase gets used as though it were a marketing term. Raw rubber's behavior is governed entirely by how freely those chains can move, and how freely they move is governed by heat. Add heat, more movement, softer. Remove heat, less movement, harder. The material has no opinion of its own; it simply obeys the temperature.

Cross-linking gives it an opinion. The sulfur bridges impose a shape that the material returns to regardless of what the thermometer says. Hot or cold, within reason, vulcanized rubber remembers what it is supposed to be.

Molecular seatbelts. That is genuinely what they are.

Goodyear was not lucky instead of persistent. He was lucky because he had been persistent.

He had the right ingredients on his bench for years. The accident only revealed the order to put them in. He patented it in 1844 and named it after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire — a rather grand name for something a man found by ruining his stove.

II · The Pneumatic Tire

Air is the best suspension component ever devised, and it is free.

You know the name Dunlop. John Boyd Dunlop, Scottish vet, working in Belfast, 1888, air-filled tire for his son's tricycle. He wrapped a wooden disc in a rubber tube, encased it in rubberized sailcloth and tacked the whole thing to the wheel. A cyclist named Willie Hume took a set to the races and won 7 of 8. An empire followed; Dunlop opened his first tire plant in 1890.

Here is the part nobody prints on the sidewall. In 1890 Dunlop's patent was withdrawn — because a fellow Scot, Robert William Thomson, had patented the pneumatic tire in 1845. Forty-three years earlier. Thomson's version worked. It was simply expensive, and the rubber of 1845 could not survive normal use.

Thomson was right and early, which in engineering is functionally indistinguishable from being wrong. Dunlop was right and on time.

The tire that mattered commercially came from Clermont-Ferrand. In 1891 Michelin patented the detachable pneumatic tire, and the significance is not romantic — it is logistical. Before Michelin, a punctured tire was glued to the rim, and repairing it took hours. After Michelin, it took minutes. Charles Terront rode a set 1,200 km (750 miles) to win the first Paris–Brest–Paris, in 71 hours and 22 minutes.

Did You Know

The following year the Michelin brothers organized a demonstration race from Paris to Clermont-Ferrand and quietly scattered nails along the route, so that every entrant would puncture and every entrant would see how quickly a Michelin could be fixed. It is remembered as the Nail Race. It is one of the great pieces of marketing in industrial history, and it was a stitch-up.

Then, in June 1895, André and Édouard entered a car in the Paris–Bordeaux–Paris — car number 46, a Peugeot chassis with a Daimler engine, named L'Éclair because its steering was so vague that it moved down the road in zigzags. It was the first automobile in history to run on air.

It punctured continuously. The brothers worked through their entire stock of spare inner tubes. Émile Levassor, who won the race outright in 48 hours 47 minutes, suggested they try filling their tires with cotton, cork or hay instead. He went on record saying air-filled tires would never be of the slightest use on a motor car.

Everyone else watching understood exactly what they had seen.

Where the sources disagree

How badly did L'Éclair actually do? Michelin's own account has the car reaching Paris ninth and last, but inside the 100-hour limit the rules allowed — one of only nine finishers from a field of about 19. Other histories say the brothers gave up after roughly 90 hours, having exhausted a stock of 22 spare inner tubes.

The "22" that circulates as a puncture count is almost certainly the tube count. What nobody disputes: the car started, the tires failed repeatedly, and within a decade every serious car in Europe was running on air.

III · Carbon Black

A pigment that turned out to be a structure.

Tires were not always black. Early tires were white, or an unhappy gray — natural rubber is pale, and manufacturers were extending it with zinc oxide.

Then somebody tried lampblack. Soot. Fine particles of elemental carbon, produced by burning hydrocarbons badly on purpose, and used for centuries in printers' ink.

It turned the rubber black, which is what everyone expected. What nobody expected was that the rubber became dramatically, almost absurdly tougher. More abrasion-resistant. More heat-resistant. Better protected against sunlight. Tire life did not improve incrementally. It improved by something on the order of ten times.

The mechanism is that carbon black particles are extraordinarily fine and enormously numerous, and the rubber chains bond to their surfaces. What was a net of polymer becomes a net of polymer anchored to millions of hard points. It stiffens. It dissipates heat. It resists being torn.

Where the sources disagree — and how it resolves

Three different accounts circulate. One credits Sidney Charles Mote, a chemist at the London-based India Rubber Company, around 1904. One credits the Silvertown Rubber Company in 1910. One credits Diamond Rubber of Akron, or B.F. Goodrich, around 1910 to 1912.

They are all the same story. Mote's employer was the India Rubber, Gutta Percha and Telegraph Works Company, whose factory stood in Silvertown, East London — so "Silvertown" and "the India Rubber Company" are one firm, not two. Mote led the team that established, around 1904, what large amounts of carbon black did to rubber's physical properties. Diamond Rubber of Akron then acquired the American rights, and Diamond's George Oenslager introduced carbon black into US tires around 1912. B.F. Goodrich bought Diamond Rubber that same year, and inherited both the patents and the credit.

The tidy irony: Goodrich's own premium tire line was named Silvertown, after the London works. The Americans bought the discovery and then named a tire after the place they bought it from.

Oenslager deserves his own line, because he is frequently miscredited. His genuinely enormous contribution was not carbon black at all — it was the discovery, in 1906, that aniline and its derivatives accelerate vulcanization, cutting cure times and energy use dramatically. Accelerators are the reason a tire can be cured in minutes rather than hours, and the reason synthetic rubber could later be vulcanized at all.

There is a footnote here that explains why your grandfather's tires had white sidewalls. Carbon black went into the tread first and was not thought worth putting in the sidewall, because in a cloth-reinforced tire the fabric wore out before the sidewall rubber did. Once cords replaced woven cloth, the sidewalls got carbon black too, and the all-black tire arrived.

Which is the point. Both of the discoveries that made the modern tire possible — vulcanization and carbon black — were found rather than designed. The tire is a happy accident wearing a lab coat.

An interruption, for the cords

Between carbon black and the tubeless tire sits a change that nobody puts on a list of breakthroughs and everybody should. Early tires used woven canvas as reinforcement, and woven cloth has a fatal habit: as the tire flexes, the threads saw against each other and grind themselves to death from the inside.

In June 1892 an American named John F. Palmer patented a remedy — a "thread-fabric" tire using unwoven cords running parallel, each cord encased in rubber so nothing rubbed against anything else. He moved to England, registered the Palmer Tyre Company, opened a plant in Silvertown in 1895, and by around 1903 was making cord tires for automobiles. Palmer Aero built the first cord airplane tires, an application where the punishment of a landing made cord construction essential rather than optional.

B.F. Goodrich acquired Palmer's US patents in 1898 and eventually turned them into the Silvertown Cord, one of the most successful early cord tires in America. Cord tires were thicker, more durable, lower in rolling resistance and considerably harsher-riding than the fabric tires they replaced, which is why they were used on airplanes and electric cars first and took until the 1910s to win over ordinary buyers. Then Dunlop's steel bead and woven cord casing tripled tire life again in 1922.

The tire stopped being made and started being engineered.

IV · The Tubeless Tire

Remove the thing most likely to kill you. It only took half a century.

For the first sixty years of the pneumatic tire, the air lived in an inner tube, and the tube was the weak link. Natural rubber leaks. A tube chafes against the inside of the casing, generates heat, and when it fails it fails instantly — because there is nothing sealing the tire to the rim except the tube itself. A blowout at speed in 1935 was not a puncture. It was an event.

Everyone could see the answer. Goodyear patented a tubeless automobile tire in 1903. Killen Tire filed in 1928 and was granted a British patent in 1930. Continental patented a tubeless concept in 1943. None of them could make it work, for the same tedious reason that stopped everything else here: the rubber of the day leaked.

The fix required a synthetic that did not exist yet — butyl rubber, hard, unlovely, and effectively impermeable to air. Bond it to the inside of the casing as an inner liner, seal the bead against the rim, and the casing itself becomes the pressure vessel. Goodyear got there through Chemigum, its wartime synthetic. Frank Herzegh at B.F. Goodrich filed in 1946 and Goodrich announced in 1947.

The rollout is a lovely piece of caution. Work had started during the war on military vehicles. The civilian version was tested on taxicabs and police cars — fleets that rack up abuse fast and complain loudly — then released in selected markets in 1948, sold nationally by 1950, and by 1955 tubeless tires were standard on almost all new cars. Goodyear's Tubeless DeLuxe Super-Cushion of 1954 was the first fitted as standard equipment.

The advertising from those years is unusually good, because for once the claims were testable. Goodrich published AAA-certified results: tires weakened with knife cuts to force a failure, where every tube-type tire blew out and collapsed instantly, while the tubeless ones bled air slowly and ran up to eight miles after failing, giving the driver up to 10 minutes and 57 seconds to bring the car to a safe stop. Separately, tires pierced through by 3-inch spikes did not lose a pound of air.

Goodyear's counter-ad hammered ten nails into each of four tires, bolted them to a Jimmie Lynch Death Dodger stunt car, and drove it off a ramp. Total damage: one shaken driver.

Where the sources disagree

The Petersen credits Vredestein's Profilux Tubeless of 1955 as Europe's first tubeless tire. Vredestein's own corporate history is more careful, saying only that it was one of the first manufacturers in Europe to produce them. Given Continental's 1943 patent and the number of European firms working the same problem, the softer claim is the safer one.

Worth knowing either way: the Profilux grew out of the R7, whose tread used a design patented in 1937 by B.F. Goodrich, and Vredestein's car tire factory at Enschede was founded jointly with B.F. Goodrich. The tubeless tire is not an American story with a European footnote. It is the same story, told in two languages.

Goodrich also had to defend the patent in court repeatedly, precisely because so many people had gotten there first on paper. Being first to file is not the same as being first to succeed, and in this industry it is barely even related.

V · The Radial

The architecture of every passenger tire on Earth. Filed in secret, during a war, to fix a Citroën.

A bias-ply tire is built from cords laid diagonally, criss-crossing from bead to bead at 30 to 60 degrees. It is simple and it is strong, and it has one fatal compromise: the tread and the sidewall are the same structure. Flex the sidewall in a corner and you deform the tread. Stiffen the tread for wear and you stiffen the ride. Every improvement in one is paid for by the other.

Michelin's engineers had been trying to bond steel to rubber since the 1930s — six years of work before they managed it permanently, producing the steel-cased Metalic in 1937. What they realized next was that if you could put steel belts beneath the tread, running around the circumference, then you could lay the carcass cords straight across the tire at ninety degrees and let the two structures do entirely different jobs.

The tread band, held rigid by the belts, stays flat on the road. The sidewall, no longer required to support the tread, is free to be soft.

Here is the part the histories usually leave out. Michelin owned Citroën at the time, and Citroën had a specific, expensive, front-wheel-drive problem: its cars ate their front tires. The most important structural idea in tire history was, in part, a warranty-cost exercise.

The patent was filed on 4 June 1946. It went on sale in October 1949 as the Michelin X. It lasted two to three times as long as a bias-ply tire, it rolled with less resistance, and it steered with a precision nobody had experienced. Europe adopted it almost immediately.

America says no, at length

The standard version of this story is that American manufacturers refused to retool. That is true, and it is not the whole truth. Radials also rode harder and noisier at low speed, which meant the car makers had to retune suspensions to accept them. It was not one industry dragging its feet. It was two.

So America invented a compromise nobody remembers: the bias-belted tire. Keep the angled bias plies, add a belt under the tread like a radial. No new tire machinery, no new suspension engineering, a decent fraction of the wear benefit. Goodyear's Polyglas paired a polyester cord body with a fiberglass belt and claimed, in a back-to-back test over 20,027 miles, that the Polyglas still had plenty of tread while the comparison tire was nearly bald.

An entire tire architecture existed for roughly a decade for the sole purpose of avoiding capital expenditure. Then it vanished.

The dam broke fast. B.F. Goodrich released the Silvertown Radial 900 in 1965 and the Radial 990 in 1967, but no automaker would fit them as standard. Then in 1968 came the improved Lifesaver Radial, and — decisively — a Consumer Reports endorsement of radial tires. Sales took off. By 1970 Ford was making radials standard on some models. The rush to convert factories killed or sold off a generation of smaller American tire companies.

Goodrich, having moved first, stayed independent until 1988, when it sold its tire business to Michelin. The one American firm that bet early on the French architecture was eventually bought by the French.

The tire on your car this morning is a radial. The tire on your car in 2040 will almost certainly still be one.

Look at that chart for a second, because it is the argument of this entire piece. Almost nothing in the tire was invented when you think it was. The ideas arrived early, sat on a shelf, and waited — sometimes for a century — until a material showed up that could carry them.

The Sixth Breakthrough

The One Nobody Ranks

In February 1942 the United States lost more than 90% of its rubber, and had months, not years, to invent a replacement or lose the war.

Every list of tire breakthroughs stops at five. Vulcanization, pneumatic, carbon black, tubeless, radial. It is a good list and it is missing the only one that decided a war.

Start with the part that makes the rest unforgivable: America had already done it, and put it down because it was expensive.

1934: the tire that was eight years early

On 21 June 1934, the Associated Press reported from Wilmington, Delaware that the first American synthetic rubber automobile tires were ready. They were built by the Dayton Rubber Manufacturing Company of Dayton, Ohio, using DuPont's Neoprene — a synthetic made from acetylene, itself made from coal and limestone. Every ingredient domestic. Not one ounce of natural rubber in the tire.

The wire copy is startling to read now. The tires were described as a check against excessive rubber prices and a guarantee of American rubber independence in wartime. In 1934. The news went around the world in newspapers, newsreels and trade journals.

Then it died, for the dullest possible reason. Synthetic rubber cost about $1 a pound (roughly $25 today). Imported natural rubber cost about 15 cents (roughly $3.70). The Depression had gutted tire demand anyway. Dayton shelved the program and went back to selling V-belts.

Goodyear's parallel effort ran the same way. Chemigum, its petroleum-derived synthetic, finally emerged in 1938 after roughly two decades of work — and Goodyear's own wartime advertising admits, in print, that it was still difficult to make in quantity and still relatively expensive. The same ad closes by telling readers that saving rubber is a vital national duty. Quantity production of Chemigum tires did not begin until 1943, and most of it went to the military.

Then the tap closed

Roosevelt had seen it coming. In June 1940 he created the Rubber Reserve Company, told Americans to conserve, imposed a national "Victory Speed" limit to make tires last, and began stockpiling. It was not enough. In 1940, synthetic rubber accounted for 0.4% of American consumption.

Before the war, the plantations of British Malaya, the Dutch East Indies, British India and French Indochina accounted for 96% of world rubber production. The Dutch East Indies alone was about 35% of world supply. Malaya had been the largest single producer since the 1930s. Attempts to develop rubber outside the Far East had reached about 5% of American crude rubber imports by the start of the war.

Between December 1941 and February 1942, Japan took Malaya, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies. Singapore — the port, the entrepôt, the place the rubber left from — fell on 15 February 1942. In a matter of weeks the United States lost over 90% of its supply, and had no domestic latex, no meaningful alternative source, and no substitute.

Here is the thesis, and it is worth stating plainly because it sounds like an exaggeration and is not.

Japan did not need to defeat the Allies. It needed to take two colonies and a port.

A Sherman tank required roughly a ton of rubber. A battleship, 75 tons. Every inch of military wiring was wrapped in it. Tire carcasses and treads alone consumed about 70% of all rubber inputs. There is no aircraft, no landing craft, no truck convoy, no gas mask, no self-sealing fuel tank without it. An army with no rubber is an army that walks.

The honest caveat, since this is Carveyance and not a war-gaming forum: the Allies did not actually run out, and the reason is worth knowing. Ceylon and southern India stayed in Allied hands, which is precisely why the loss was 90-something percent rather than 100. Liberia and Brazil produced small quantities. Scrap drives and speed limits stretched what was left. And the strangulation only ever had to hold for as long as it took American chemistry to catch up — which it did, at a speed nobody expected.

But for about a year, the arithmetic was genuinely terrifying, and the people doing it knew exactly what it meant.

51 factories

What followed is one of the least-celebrated industrial achievements of the twentieth century. The government, four tire companies who were bitter competitors — Firestone, Goodrich, Goodyear and U.S. Royal — the infant petrochemical industry and a dozen university laboratories were welded into a single program and told to share everything. 51 factories were built. The first alcohol-to-butadiene unit broke ground in April 1942 and was producing within ten months.

By 1950, synthetic rubber outproduced the tree.

Consider what that means. The material that had come out of the Amazon for 3,000 years, that Europe spent two centuries failing to understand, that an entire colonial economy was built to extract — was replaced, under deadline, by chemistry. Not improved. Replaced.

Did You Know

The war didn't only produce synthetic rubber. It produced the tubeless tire, which needed butyl; it accelerated cord and nylon construction; and it produced the first mass-produced run-flat systems, because a military vehicle that stops is a target. Nearly every so-called 1950s breakthrough has its birth certificate stamped 1942.

And yet.

It Still Comes From a Tree

Because synthetic did not win. It drew.

The material keeping you alive at 80 mph is still, roughly half of it, the sap of Hevea brasiliensis — native to the Amazon, harvested by cutting the bark and letting the white latex run into a cup. The tree needs about six years of growth before you can tap it.

It is no longer grown where it came from. More than 90% of the world's natural rubber now comes out of Southeast Asia — Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia — plus West Africa. And it is essentially one species, with low genetic diversity, which is the sort of sentence that makes agronomists reach for a drink.

For tires specifically, Michelin puts the split closer to 60% synthetic, 40% natural. The reason is instructive.

Synthetic rubber is the engineer. You can tune it — for grip, for rolling resistance, for weather, for ozone, for oil, for air retention. The halobutyl in your inner liner is what stops the tire deflating overnight, and nothing from a tree will do that job.

Natural rubber is the gifted athlete. Nothing man-made matches it for tear resistance, fatigue resistance and low heat build-up under heavy load. Which is why — and I find this genuinely astonishing — the tread on a commercial airliner's tires is almost entirely natural rubber. The U.S. Tire Manufacturers Association is blunt about it: synthetic rubber cannot fully perform in that application.

More than 80 years of petrochemistry, 51 wartime factories, and we still cannot beat the tree where it matters most.

Mud, Snow and Worse

Tread Had to Be Invented Twice

The first automobile tires were smooth. Perfectly, gleamingly, lethally smooth. On the unpaved roads of 1900 this made driving in mud or snow a dangerous and frequently futile activity, and the tires wore out at a spectacular rate into the bargain.

The first fix came from outside the tire industry entirely. Woodworth sold bolt-on detachable treads — a leather-and-steel strip you strapped over your existing tire, advertised under the headline Prevent Punctures, with the confident claim that of the thousands of covers sold, not one had ever been punctured. The small print notes they had no equal for preventing skidding in winter. Lee Tires went further with a puncture-proof system in which layers of small metal discs were distributed among the fabric and rubber plies.

Then the tire companies took the idea in-house. Around 1904 Dunlop patented a process for pressing metal bars into the softened rubber during vulcanizing, creating grooves that ran across the tire — primitive, but a vast improvement on nothing. Around the same time Dunlop's simple Grooved Tyres reached the market, and manufacturers began copying the technique.

The real change came in 1908, when Goodyear and Firestone both began etching tread patterns directly into the curing molds, so the pattern was formed as the tire was made rather than added afterward. Goodyear's diamond-block All-Weather tread debuted that year and ran, with modifications, for 40 years.

Fun Fact

Firestone's answer was the Non-Skid tire of 1908, and its tread blocks were molded into the actual words NON-SKID, repeated around the circumference. The tire told you what it did every time it went round. The company later simplified the advertising to just "FIRESTONE NONSKID," on the grounds that the name prevents the slip.

The raised lettering wore off first, which meant that a Firestone that could no longer stop you also stopped claiming it could.

Winter, and the two countries that claim it

Early patterned treads were advertised as capable in all conditions, which was true only by comparison with a smooth tire. As cars became year-round transportation, somebody had to build a tire specifically for snow.

Two claims, same decade. In America, the Gillette Rubber Company of Eau Claire, Wisconsin — founded 1917 — introduced the Super-Traction in the early 1930s, a tread of large raised nubs designed to sink into snow and wet soil. Gillette's advertising is a small period masterpiece: the tire was pitched at farmers, mail carriers, doctors and salesmen who had to leave the main highways, it claimed to do away with troublesome chains, and the company logo was a bear with a tire, above the slogan "A Bear For Wear."

In Finland, Suomen Gummitehdas Oy — headquartered in the town of Nokia, and selling under the name Nokian — began making car tires in 1932, launched the Kelirengas in 1934 as the first truck tire developed specifically for snow, and released the passenger-car Hakkapeliitta in 1936, with a transverse tread pattern designed to bite into soft snow like teeth.

Compounds followed later: special rubbers that stay soft below freezing, which is the thing that actually makes a modern winter tire work. A summer tire in the cold is not short of tread. It is short of flexibility. The cross-links are still there, but the chains between them have stopped moving, and you are essentially driving on the 1839 problem.

Did You Know

Studded tires began as a home-brew fix. Drivers had been hammering nails and screws through their own tire carcasses for extra grip since the 19th century. Manufactured studded tires only appeared in the late 1950s. A modern studded tire carries around 100 small metal studs set into the tread to break through packed snow and ice.

Which brings us to the best failure in the whole story.

The Pirelli BS3, and the tire nobody trusted

In 1959 Pirelli introduced a genuinely elegant solution to the seasonal problem. The BS3 came with three interchangeable tread bands — summer patterns and winter patterns — that fitted over the casing and were held in place by ridges in the tire and by air pressure. No swapping tires. No wrestling with chains at the roadside in the dark. Change the band, change the season.

It worked. It performed reliably. Almost nobody bought it.

The problem was not engineering, it was imagination. Every potential customer could picture, with perfect clarity, a tread band peeling off at 60 mph. It did not matter that they never did. Production ended in 1964.

You cannot sell a tire that people can imagine failing, however well it works.

Vredestein got the same territory right two decades later. The Snow+ of 1979, offered with or without studs, was a hit that established the company as a winter-tire specialist and still underpins its reputation.

All-terrain, or how the tire made the SUV possible

In 1976 BFGoodrich released the Radial All-Terrain T/A, with a bias-ply variant alongside it. These were the first tires widely accepted as genuinely dual-purpose, and they created a category that did not previously exist.

The trick was the middle ground: an open tread that lets the blocks flex and bite loose ground, but less aggressive than a mud tire so it runs quietly on pavement, on a sidewall thicker than a road tire and thinner than an off-road one. The result made a recreational four-wheel-drive feel like a car on the highway and like a dedicated off-roader on the trail.

Every crossover on your street is descended from that compromise. So, for that matter, is the entire idea that a truck can be a family car.

The Extremes

All of which is prologue. The passenger car tire — 32 psi, 28 inches, quietly excellent — sits almost precisely in the middle of what rubber is asked to do. Travel outward in either direction and things get strange very fast.

6.5 PSI · The Drag Slick

A Top Fuel dragster makes something in the region of 11,000 horsepower and delivers all of it through two rear tires running at about 6.5 psi. Your bicycle runs more than 10 times that.

This is not an oversight. It is the entire mechanism.

At launch, torque tries to twist the tire off its beadlock rim. The sidewalls — deliberately, famously soft; the "wrinkle wall" Goodyear introduced with the Blue Streak in 1964 — crumple. The tire's radius shrinks by more than 6 inches. The tread balls up ahead of the contact patch, which swells to nearly 250 square inches. Two sheets of letter paper, side by side, pressed into the asphalt.

Now think about what has just happened. The tire has become smaller. A smaller rolling radius is a shorter final drive. The tire has re-geared the car, by deforming, at the precise instant the car needs it most.

Then it unwinds. The stored torque releases, the sidewall snaps back, and as the car accelerates, centrifugal force stretches that 36-inch tire out to as much as 38 inches. Taller gearing. Narrower patch. Lower rolling resistance. Exactly what you want at 330 mph.

By the time this is finished the driver is pulling 4 G — roughly what an astronaut feels leaving the pad.

For about a second and a half, the tire is not a component of the transmission. The tire is the transmission.

They last two to four runs. Goodyear has, for decades, been the only company that bothers to make them.

Harry Hogge would have loved a Top Fuel car. It is the only machine in motorsport where the tires do not merely win the race — they are, for a second and a half, most of the drivetrain.

200 PSI · The Aircraft Tire

Now run the other way.

A Boeing 747 tire is inflated to around 200 psi — more than six times your car. It stands 49 inches tall and weighs about 110 kg (243 lb). There are 18 of them, and here is the detail that delights me: they are all identical, nose gear included, which almost no other airliner bothers to do.

Each one is certified to carry 56,600 lb. Each is rated to 204 knots — 235 mph — because a heavy jet on rotation is doing Formula One speeds on a surface it cannot see much of.

They are filled with nitrogen rather than air, because air carries moisture and oxygen and neither behaves well when a tire cycles between minus 60 degrees Celsius at altitude and a runway in Dubai in August. Aircraft wheels also carry fusible plugs — small bolts filled with low-melting-point alloy which surrender at a predetermined temperature and deflate the tire in an orderly manner, rather than letting it detonate beside a ground crew.

The strength figures are faintly ridiculous. Dunlop tested a 737 tire well past four times its certified pressure; it went beyond 900 psi before bursting. Concorde ran 232 psi in the main gear and 294 in the tail bumper — and the extraordinary pressures and loads on those tires were a significant factor in the loss of Air France 4590.

And then, having survived all of that, the tire is retreaded. 8 to 10 times as standard. Some as many as 16. Airlines usually stop short of the manufacturer's limit, because airlines are conservative in exactly the ways that matter.

13 Feet · The Earthmover

The Michelin XDR 59/80R63 is, by consensus, the largest tire on Earth. The numbers stop making sense somewhere in the middle of the spec sheet.

It stands 4.03 meters tall — over 13 feet — and just under 5 feet wide. It weighs more than 5 tonnes; the current Extra Load version comes in at 5,350 kg (11,795 lb). That is 5 Mazda Miatas. In a tire.

It carries over 100 tonnes. By itself. Six of them go under a haul truck with a 400-ton payload and a gross weight north of 600 tonnes.

Inside it: 890 kg (1,962 lb) of steel — enough to build two small cars — and 3,850 kg (8,488 lb) of rubber, enough to make roughly 600 passenger tires. Michelin sold one in 2012 for about $42,500, which is roughly $60,000 today. You would pay about the price of a new Miata, and then own one tire.

Zero · Where Rubber Quits

Here is my favorite fact in this entire piece.

Bloodhound LSR is built to travel at 1,000 mph. It does not have tires. Not small ones, not special ones, not exotic compounds — none. It runs on solid forged aluminum discs.

Andy Green, the man who drove Thrust SSC through the sound barrier in 1997 and still holds the record at 763 mph, puts it plainly: above roughly 450 mph, rubber gets flung off the rim. There is no compound, no construction, no belt package that survives it. Centrifugal force simply removes the tread from the tire and throws it at the desert.

So: four aluminum wheels, 95 kg (209 lb) each, 36 inches across, spinning at 10,200 rpm, enduring 50,000 g at the rim. Fifty thousand. A bag of sugar resting on that rim would weigh as much as a fully loaded articulated lorry.

Above 400 mph the wheels stop steering the car in any meaningful sense and begin to behave like rudders, cutting into the salt.

We spent 180 years perfecting rubber. Then we went fast enough that rubber said no.

And Two That Left the Planet

The Moon. The Lunar Roving Vehicle was developed by General Motors Defense Research Laboratories and Boeing, and used on the final three Apollo missions in 1971 and 1972. It remains the only vehicle ever driven by humans on the surface of another celestial body.

Its tires are woven from zinc-coated steel piano wire — each strand about three-hundredths of an inch thick — with titanium chevrons riveted across the tread to stop the wheels sinking into the soft lunar soil. A rigid metal inner frame prevented the mesh from over-deforming. No air. No rubber. Lunar soil proved firmer than expected; the tracks are only about half an inch deep. They are still there.

That last pair of numbers is the whole of lunar engineering in two lines. Everything the rover carried weighed one sixth of what it weighs here, and everything it was built to survive had to be reckoned in Earth terms anyway, because that is where it was tested, and where it had to survive being launched.

Read next $38 Million and One Horsepower

The full story of the machine those wheels were bolted to — what it cost, what it could do, and why four of them are still parked up there.

Mars. Curiosity landed in 2012 on rigid aluminum wheels. Within a year, engineers watching the downlinked images noticed the wheels were tearing. Not wearing — tearing. Martian ventifacts, wind-sharpened rocks welded into the ground, and a rover powerful enough to drive over them rather than around.

NASA Glenn's answer, developed with Goodyear in 2008, was the Spring Tire: an airless tire woven from several hundred coiled spring-steel wires, explicitly modeled on the Apollo rover tires, durable enough to carry heavy loads and flexible enough to conform to rough ground. The example that survives was built for "Chariot," a large pressurized rover prototype at Johnson Space Center in 2010. Later NASA mesh tires swapped the spring steel for shape-memory alloys, which deform completely around an obstacle and then remember their own shape.

Which is, when you squint, precisely what Charles Goodyear's sulfur bridges do. Stretch, and come back.

We took the idea to another planet, ran out of rubber, and rebuilt the idea in metal.

The Tire Learns to Speak

For 100 years the tire was mute. It told you something was wrong only after you could feel it — vibration, a pull, a bang.

That changed for an ugly reason. Through 1999 and 2000, tread began separating from Firestone tires fitted to Ford Explorers. The vehicles rolled. More than 100 people died. In August 2000 Firestone recalled 6.5 million tires; both companies pointed at each other; congressional hearings followed in September. Congress passed the TREAD Act in an 18-hour span and Clinton signed it on 1 November 2000.

Buried in it was a provision requiring every new light vehicle sold in America to warn its driver of a significantly under-inflated tire. Phase-in began in 2005. From 1 September 2007 it was universal. The little horseshoe with the exclamation mark on your dashboard exists because 100 people died and Congress moved faster than it has moved since.

TPMS is crude. It shouts only when a tire is already 25% down. What comes next is not.

Continental's fleet systems already stream pressure, temperature, mileage and tread depth in real time. Pirelli's Cyber Tyre embeds a sensor in the carcass and pipes data to the vehicle's electronics. In 2024 Pirelli and Bosch announced they would develop intelligent-tire technology together, and in 2026 Pirelli bought 30% of the Swedish AI firm Univrses to push the same work further.

Think about what that solves. Your car's ABS, stability control, traction control, torque vectoring, adaptive cruise, autonomous emergency braking and regenerative braking are all making decisions about grip while being structurally unable to feel any. They infer. They estimate. They model. Meanwhile the one component actually touching the road says nothing at all.

The endgame is a car that knows, rather than guesses: these are winter tires, it is 42°F, the left rear is down 4 psi, the rears are worn, road friction is low, and you are entering this corner too quickly. And then softens the throttle before you have finished being wrong.

The Oldest New Problem

Everyone will tell you electric cars created the low-rolling-resistance tire. Electric cars created it in about 1912.

At the very beginning of automotive history, electric motors were as common as gasoline engines, and tire manufacturers tailored their products to each. Electric cars were heavy, so they were often fitted with solid rubber rather than the fragile pneumatics of the day, and the penalty for solid rubber was rolling resistance — which, on a battery car, is range.

So Firestone built a dual-cushion solid rubber tire specifically for electric vehicles in the early 1910s, with a double tread to improve cushioning and lower rolling resistance. The advertisement, in Country Life in America for December 1912, is addressed "To Electric Car Owners" and leads with two claims in large type: 12% more miles on battery charge, and 12% more resilience.

Read that again. A tire sold on range, to electric car buyers, in 1912.

The thread never breaks, it just goes quiet for decades at a time:

  • 1979. After the oil crisis, Goodyear builds a special set of low-rolling-resistance tires for the GE-Chrysler ETV-1, a DOE-sponsored electric test vehicle. NASA later track-tested them against standard commercial tires to characterize exactly what the difference was worth.
  • 1996. GM chooses Michelin to supply the EV1. The Proxima RR debuts on that car, run at very high pressure to cut rolling resistance by 25%, with a puncture sealant under the tread so the car did not have to carry a heavy spare.
  • 2008. The Swiss Mindset E-Motion hybrid concept runs narrow 22-inch wheels wearing ultra-low-profile Vredesteins, the odd sizes chosen purely for aerodynamics and rolling resistance.

Rolling resistance is the energy a tire loses simply by being a tire. Rubber is viscoelastic: when you deform it, you do not get all the energy back. Every rotation, the contact patch flattens and un-flattens, the sidewall bends and un-bends, and a fraction of that work leaves as heat. In a combustion car, that loss is trivial noise beside an engine that is throwing away two-thirds of its fuel as heat anyway.

In an EV there is nowhere to hide it. Rolling resistance is range, directly and legibly, on a display in front of the driver.

And EVs make the tire's life harder in every other respect. They are heavy, because batteries are heavy. They deliver maximum torque from a standstill. They are quiet, so you hear the tires. J.D. Power's 2024 tire study found EV owners reporting faster tire wear and attributed it squarely to weight and torque. The OECD notes the same grim trade: an EV eliminates tailpipe emissions and reduces brake wear through regeneration — but tire and road wear can go up, because the thing weighs more.

So the tire engineer is now asked for a compound that is simultaneously sticky enough to stop 2.5 tonnes, hard enough to survive instant torque, quiet enough not to intrude on a silent cabin, and slippery enough — in the rolling-resistance sense — to protect the range figure the entire car was sold on.

The tire stopped being a wear item. It became part of the energy system. Again.

Twenty Years, Sixteen Seconds, Same Car

The cleanest proof that any of this matters, because everything except the tires was held still.

Everything in this article is a claim about progress, and claims about progress are hard to test, because cars change. Engines get better, aero gets better, dampers get cleverer, and the tires improve underneath all of it without anybody being able to say how much of the gain belongs to them.

Then Porsche ran the experiment properly, by accident.

The Carrera GT went out of production in 2006. In 2024, dealing with a suspension recall on a car two decades old, Porsche had Michelin develop a bespoke set of Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires for it and supplied them to owners. Then Sport Auto took a yellow one to the Nordschleife with Porsche factory driver Jörg Bergmeister at the wheel and Manthey Racing running the pit box.

Same car. Same 5.7-liter V10, same six-speed manual, same near-total absence of aerodynamic assistance, same rear-wheel drive, same 20.6 km lap. The only meaningful variable was the rubber.

7:12.69.

That is 16 seconds faster than Walter Röhrl managed in 2004 on the tires the car left the factory wearing, and 20 seconds faster than Horst von Saurma's 7:32 in the 2003 Sport Auto Supertest. It also put a 2004 supercar ahead of several considerably newer and more sophisticated performance cars on the same measure.

Be honest about the caveats, because they exist. Bergmeister is not Röhrl, and both are extraordinary. The 2003 run had damp patches. And the Nordschleife has been resurfaced and revised repeatedly in 20 years, which is worth a few seconds all by itself. Nobody should pretend the tires banked the whole 16.

But they banked most of it, and the more interesting numbers are not the lap times at all. Michelin's figure for the new tire is that it stops the car from 200 km/h (124 mph) in 12 meters (39 feet) less than the original.

Thirty-nine feet is not a lap record. Thirty-nine feet is the difference between a near miss and a crash.

That is what this entire history has actually been buying, breakthrough by accidental breakthrough. Vulcanization, carbon black, cords, the tubeless casing, the radial, silica, the modern multi-compound tread with one rubber on the inner shoulder for wet grip and another on the outer for dry — none of it was really about going faster. Going faster is the byproduct.

What it was about is a car that turns when you ask it to, stays pointed where you put it, and stops 39 feet sooner. The Carrera GT did not get better in 2024. The four postcards did.

The Airless Question, Which Is 127 Years Old

Which brings us, inevitably, to the idea of simply getting rid of the air.

Everybody presents this as the future. It is, in fact, one of the oldest ideas in the industry, and it has lost every single time.

Pneumatic tires of the 1890s were wonderful and infuriating: better ride, better grip, and a puncture rate that made every journey provisional. Changing a flat took real effort. So manufacturers built alternatives, and they built a lot of them.

The Lattina Cellular Tire, introduced around 1899, was the most sophisticated of the early airless designs: solid rubber layered with fabric and an inner structure of open chambers that behaved like an air-filled inner tube. The cavities formed an arch, keeping the tire rigid while allowing it to flex. Its advertising promised no inflation, no leaky valves, no punctures, and it is now recognized as a direct precursor to the modern Michelin Tweel.

Others followed. The Lambert Tire and Rubber Company, founded in Portland, Oregon in 1913, opened its main factory in Akron in 1919 and made the "Trublpruf," a non-pneumatic tire with open cells for cushioning. It sold. Kelly Springfield built one in 1925; Wards Riverside had one by 1930.

They all lost, and the reason is speed. Non-pneumatic tires create more rolling resistance and cannot dissipate the heat of road friction as well as air-filled tires can. As cars got faster, airless tires were phased out of passenger use — surviving only where speed was not the point, which is why forklifts still run on them.

Did You Know

Michelin introduced the Tweel as a concept at the 2004 Paris Motor Show: a conventional tread over a shear beam, connected to a rigid hub by flexible, deformable polyurethane spokes. That is 105 years after the Lattina Cellular Tire, and it is essentially the same argument, rebuilt in materials that can survive it.

The Tweel is on sale today — for UTVs, golf carts, and low-speed utility vehicles. Automotive versions remain under development. Exactly as in 1899.

The modern attempt is more serious. Michelin's UPTIS prototypes have covered nearly 3 million km (1.9 million miles) in real fleet service since 2020, in Singapore, the United States and France. No punctures. No blowouts. No underinflation. No roadside stops, and no tires scrapped early because somebody drove them flat. Bridgestone's AirFree uses recyclable thermoplastic resin spokes and is designed from the outset to be retreaded and recycled.

And the most interesting entrant is the one that came back from the Moon. The SMART Tire Company, using NASA-developed technology, has built prototype airless tires from Nitinol — a nickel-titanium shape memory alloy with the elasticity of rubber and the strength of titanium, which returns to its original shape after deformation without losing integrity, and weighs considerably less than rubber. On production versions, the metal mesh gets wrapped in a rubber and polymer tread and sidewall.

Which means the descendant of the Apollo rover wheel is being productized as a road tire, and the first thing they did to it was put rubber back on.

So why aren't they on your car?

Because air is astonishing. It is free. It is weightless. It is infinitely adjustable with a hand pump. And it absorbs impacts better than anything we have ever engineered to replace it — because a gas under pressure is a perfect spring, and a spoke is not.

Spokes transmit what air would have swallowed. Open structures generate noise and resonance, and they trap stones and mud and snow. Sustained highway speed builds heat in a structure with nowhere to put it. Some airless designs are heavier. All of them are more expensive. And sidewall flex — the thing a radial tire spent 70 years learning to tune — is much harder to control without a sidewall.

The near future is not your daily driver. It is postal vans, airport tugs, construction plant, military vehicles, low-speed shuttles, lawn tractors — every application in which a flat tire is an expensive scheduling problem rather than a ride-quality one.

Your car gets airless tires the day they match air for comfort, noise, cost, heat, weight and range. Which is a tall order, because air has had a 138-year head start and has never once been beaten.

The Bill

Roughly 3 billion tires are produced every year, and this is where the romance runs out.

As tires roll, brake, corner and scrub, they shed. The EPA estimates a single tire sheds somewhere between 2 and 14 lb of rubber over its life. The industry calls the result tire and road wear particles — roughly half tread, half pavement, about 100 microns across, the thickness of a human hair. The fine fraction goes airborne. The rest goes down a storm drain.

Then there is 6PPD. It is an antiozonant: it stops rubber cracking, which is a genuine safety function and not a nicety — ozone attacks the cross-links that Goodyear built. But when 6PPD meets ozone it can form 6PPD-quinone, which washes off roads into streams. A 2021 paper in Science tied coho salmon die-offs to it. The EPA states that available information indicates 6PPD-quinone is toxic enough to kill some fish quickly.

A chemical that keeps your tire from failing is killing salmon. That is the actual trade, stated plainly, and the industry is scrambling for an alternative that does the first job without the second.

Recycling helps and does not close the loop. Vulcanization is the problem it always was: cross-linked rubber will not un-cross-link. You cannot melt a tire back into a tire the way you melt a can back into a can. So end-of-life tires become fuel — 33% of use in 2023 — and ground rubber, 28%. Rubber-modified asphalt. Playground surfaces. Athletic fields. Vibration damping. Recovered carbon black, through pyrolysis. Retreads for trucks, buses and aircraft.

The most poetic outcome is rubberized asphalt, where the tire goes back into the road that wore it out.

Though the one I keep thinking about is the playground. Those soft, dark, faintly springy surfaces that replaced the concrete of my childhood are, in very large part, made of ground-up tires. The thing that spent 100,000 miles being the only part of the car touching the road gets a second career catching children.

The tire swing was never the only tire on that playground. It was just the only one still shaped like a tire.

And the tree is under pressure from three directions at once. Reuters reported in 2025 that natural rubber production was set to fall short of consumption for a fifth consecutive year — weather, insufficient replanting, and farmers switching to palm oil, which pays better. At least 2 million hectares of forest have been converted to rubber plantation since 2000. Over 6 million farmers, most of them smallholders, depend on the crop.

There is no synthetic substitute waiting in the wings. USTMA is explicit: if natural rubber supply were seriously disrupted, there is not enough synthetic capacity on Earth to cover the gap. The alternatives — guayule, and a rubber-producing dandelion — have both made successful experimental tires, and neither is remotely close to global scale. Bridgestone has invested in guayule with a stated goal of tires made from 100% sustainable materials by 2050.

Those 40,000 products from the start of this story — the hoses, the belts, the surgical gloves, the shoes — are all drawing on the same crop. It was never only a car problem.

And if that sounds familiar, it should. In 1941 the industrialized world depended on one crop, from one region, with no substitute at scale. In 2026 it depends on one species, from one region, with no substitute at scale. We solved this once, at national-emergency speed, and then quietly walked back into it.

Keeping Classics Rolling

One last problem, and it is the one most likely to affect anyone reading this.

Rubber degrades. That means driving on old stock — even unused, even beautiful, even still in the wrapper — is out of the question on anything more than a few years old. And many of the sizes that fit older cars simply are not made for current models, while modern tires look wrong on a classic.

The problem became urgent after the Second World War, when tires for Brass Era cars stopped being mass-produced at all. Through the 1950s and '60s, companies including PJA Pneumatic, Coker, Universal and the Lester Tire Company began remanufacturing defunct tire models, or building new tires in old sizes using modern technology. Today some of the major manufacturers have joined in, remaking their own historic designs or producing modern tires with a vintage look.

Which means the past needs new tires too. Everything does.

The Whole Story, in Order

  1. c. 2000 BCE
    Western Asia · Mesoamerica

    Spoked wooden wheels appear on Sintashta chariots; by the Iron Age, wheelwrights are shrinking metal hoops around them. The first tire is a band that protects the wheel, not the passenger. Half a world away, indigenous peoples are already processing latex into balls, footwear and waterproofing — some 3,000 years before Europe notices.

  2. 1736 · 1770
    Paris · England

    La Condamine ships samples back from the Amazon and Europe finally has the material, with no idea what to do with it. Joseph Priestley notes that the stuff rubs out pencil marks. It gets called rubber — a miracle polymer, named after the least interesting thing it does.

  3. 1839 · 1844
    Woburn, Massachusetts

    Charles Goodyear drops sulfur-laced rubber on a hot stove. It hardens instead of melting. Vulcanization — patented 1844.

  4. 1845
    Scotland

    Robert William Thomson patents the pneumatic tire. It works. It costs too much, and the rubber of 1845 cannot survive the road. The world shrugs.

  5. 1850s · 1886
    London · Mannheim

    Solid rubber tires for horse-drawn vehicles, with wire embedded from the 1870s to stop them stretching off the wheel; the first widespread use is on London Hansom cabs from 1881. In 1886 Carl Benz runs his Patent Motorwagen on solid rubber over metal spokes, on rims of his own design — which makes him the world's first automobile tire manufacturer, more or less by accident.

  6. 1888 · 1890
    Belfast

    John Boyd Dunlop, a vet, reinvents the pneumatic tire for his son's tricycle. Willie Hume wins 7 of 8 races on them. In 1890 the patent is withdrawn — Thomson got there 43 years earlier — and Dunlop keeps the empire anyway.

  7. 1891 · 1892
    Clermont-Ferrand

    Michelin patents the detachable pneumatic tire; repair time falls from hours to minutes. Terront rides one 1,200 km to win Paris–Brest–Paris. The following year, the Nail Race.

  8. 1895
    Paris–Bordeaux–Paris

    The Michelin brothers enter L'Éclair, the first car ever to run on air. Endless punctures. Levassor suggests they try cork or hay. It is the most important bad result in automotive history.

  9. 1899
    Philadelphia

    The Lattina Cellular Tire — solid rubber with internal chambers, no inflation, no valves, no punctures. The first serious airless tire, and a direct ancestor of the Tweel.

  10. c. 1904
    Silvertown, London

    John F. Palmer's 1892 patent for unwoven cord construction ends the woven-canvas problem, and he opens a plant at Silvertown. At the same works, S.C. Mote's team establishes what large amounts of carbon black do to rubber; tire life improves roughly tenfold. Diamond Rubber of Akron takes the American rights, and carbon black enters US tires around 1912. Meanwhile Dunlop presses metal bars into tread during vulcanizing, creating the first molded grooves.

  11. 1906 · 1908
    United States

    Fisk patents the bolted-on removable rim (1902) and demountable rims spread. In 1908 Goodyear and Firestone begin etching tread patterns into the curing molds. Goodyear's All-Weather diamond tread runs 40 years; Firestone's has NON-SKID molded into the blocks.

  12. 1910s
    Akron

    Firestone sells dual-cushion solid tires to electric car owners on a promise of 12% more miles per battery charge. Low rolling resistance is an EV selling point more than a century before anyone calls it that.

  13. 1922 · 1923
    Birmingham · Akron

    Dunlop's steel bead and woven cord casing treble tire life. Firestone pioneers the balloon tire, dropping pressures from 60 psi and higher to 30–40 psi. Ride comfort arrives.

  14. 1930s
    Wisconsin · Finland

    Gillette's Super-Traction and Nokian's Kelirengas and Hakkapeliitta: the first tires built specifically for mud and snow, on two continents at once.

  15. 1934
    Dayton, Ohio · Clermont-Ferrand

    Dayton Rubber builds the first American all-synthetic tire from DuPont Neoprene, and shelves it because synthetic costs $1 a pound against 15 cents for natural. The same year, Michelin patents a run-flat rim and tire; too complex and costly for civilians, it goes military only.

  16. 1935 · 1937
    Akron · Clermont-Ferrand

    Goodyear's LifeGuard tube — a tube within a tube, developed across 1,300 test constructions — lets a blown tire deflate slowly enough to stop safely. Michelin sells the Metalic, the first steel-cased tire, after 6 years spent bonding steel to rubber.

  17. Feb 1942
    Singapore

    Japan takes Southeast Asia. The United States loses over 90% of its natural rubber supply in a matter of weeks. A tank needs a ton of the stuff. A battleship needs 75.

  18. 1942–45
    51 factories

    The US synthetic rubber program goes from 3,721 tons a year to 756,042. Four rival tire companies are ordered to share everything. By 1950, synthetic outproduces the tree. Petrochemistry replaces agriculture.

  19. 4 June 1946
    Paris Patent Office

    Michelin files the radial — partly to stop Citroën, which it owns, from eating its front tires. Cords run across the tire, steel belts stabilize the tread, and the sidewall is freed to flex independently.

  20. 1947 · 1954
    Akron

    Goodyear patents a tubeless automobile tire in 1903 and can do nothing with it; the rubber leaks. 51 years later it is universal. B.F. Goodrich announces the tubeless tire in 1947, built around butyl, tested on taxicabs and police cars, sold regionally in 1948 and nationally by 1950. Goodyear's Tubeless DeLuxe Super-Cushion is the first fitted as standard equipment, in 1954.

  21. Oct 1949 · 1955
    Paris · Enschede

    The radial goes on sale as the Michelin X. Europe adopts it almost immediately. Vredestein's Profilux Tubeless follows in 1955, among the first tubeless tires made in Europe.

  22. 1959 · 1964
    Milan · Pontiac

    The Pirelli BS3 offers three interchangeable tread bands for summer and winter. It works; nobody trusts it; production ends in 1964.

  23. 1965 · 1968 · 1970
    United States

    Goodrich builds the first American radial. No automaker will fit it. Then Consumer Reports endorses radials in 1968, Ford makes them standard on some models by 1970, and the scramble to retool kills off a generation of smaller tire firms.

  24. 1966 · 1976
    Akron

    Firestone's Super Sports Wide Oval — lower, wider, a race tire for the street — is widely considered the first true high-performance tire. A decade later BFGoodrich's Radial All-Terrain T/A invents the dual-purpose category and, with it, the modern SUV.

  25. 1971–72
    The Moon

    The Lunar Roving Vehicle, built by GM Defense Research Laboratories and Boeing, drives on woven zinc-coated piano wire with riveted titanium chevrons. Each tire is designed to carry 60 lb on the Moon — 360 lb on Earth. The tracks are still there.

  26. 1973 · 1979
    Birmingham · Enschede

    Dunlop's Denovo: stiff sidewalls, locked beads, and canisters in the wheel that release lubricant, seal small punctures and reinflate the tire to 5 psi. Tested by detonating a charge on a moving car. Vredestein's Snow+ makes winter tires a specialism.

  27. 1988 · 1992
    Akron · Clermont-Ferrand

    Goodrich, the first American company into radials, sells its tire business to Michelin. Michelin launches its first energy-saving tire, and silica compounds begin the low-rolling-resistance era in earnest.

  28. Aug 2000
    Washington

    Firestone recalls 6.5 million tires; tread separation on Ford Explorers is linked to more than 100 deaths. Congress passes the TREAD Act in an 18-hour span.

  29. 2004 · Sept 2007
    Paris · Every new car

    Michelin shows the Tweel — airless, spoked, 105 years after the Lattina. TPMS becomes mandatory on all US light vehicles. For the first time, the tire is legally required to speak.

  30. 2008 · 2010
    NASA Glenn · Michelin

    The NASA/Goodyear Spring Tire revives the Apollo wire-mesh idea in coiled spring steel; one is built for the Chariot rover prototype in 2010. The same year, Michelin's XDR 59/80R63: 13 feet tall, 5 tonnes, 100 tonnes of load on one tire.

  31. 2019 →
    Everywhere

    UPTIS and AirFree in fleet service. A 20-year-old Carrera GT goes 16 seconds quicker around the Nordschleife on nothing but new tires. Sensors in the carcass. Nitinol shape-memory prototypes bringing the Moon tire back to Earth. 6PPD in the salmon streams. The tire becomes a computer, and a problem.

Bounces Off Me, Sticks to You

Sap from a tree in the Amazon. Soot from burning something badly. Sulfur, discovered on a ruined stove in Massachusetts. Steel wire, nylon, halobutyl, silica, polyester. Over 100 ingredients, cooked into a black ring, produced 3 billion times a year.

Asked to hold everything together at 6.5 psi or 294. At 13 feet tall or 28 inches. On asphalt, on regolith, on the surface of Mars. Through a world war that nearly ran out of it, and a supply chain that still depends on one species of tree.

Right up to the precise speed at which it gives up and flies off the rim.

And nearly every part of it was invented decades before we could build it, shelved because it was expensive, and then rediscovered by somebody who needed it badly enough — a war, an oil crisis, a lawsuit, a dead run of salmon, a rover on Mars with its wheels torn open.

The playground rhyme had it backwards, and it took me about 40 years to notice.

You don't want it to bounce off. You want it to stick.
